title: Exposition of a New Theory on the Measurement of Risk
venue: Econometrica 22(1), 23-36 (English translation by Louise Sommer of the 1738 Latin original, Specimen Theoriae Novae de Mensura Sortis, Commentarii Academiae Scientiarum Imperialis Petropolitanae vol. 5)
summary: Bernoulli asked why sensible people refuse to pay much to play a coin-tossing game whose average payout is infinite (the St. Petersburg puzzle posed by his cousin Nicolas), and why people buy insurance that costs more than the average loss it covers. His answer was that what matters is not the money an outcome brings but how useful that money is to the person, and an extra coin means less to someone who already has many. He proposed that the benefit of a small gain is inversely proportional to the wealth already held, which makes the usefulness of wealth grow like its logarithm. The rule: instead of ranking a gamble by its expected value, the sum of p_i * x_i over outcomes, rank it by its expected log-wealth, the sum of p_i * log(W + x_i), where W is current wealth; a risky prospect is worth the sure amount that gives the same expected log-wealth. Under this rule the St. Petersburg game is worth only a modest sum, insurance can make sense for both buyer and seller, and a merchant does better by splitting goods across several ships. He also credited Gabriel Cramer with a similar idea reached independently. Caveat: Karl Menger later showed that games with even faster-growing payouts defeat log utility too, and Kahneman and Tversky's prospect theory found that people judge gains and losses relative to a reference point rather than total wealth, so the log rule is a useful norm rather than a description of behavior.

title: Théorie de la spéculation
venue: Annales scientifiques de l'École Normale Supérieure, 3e série, 17, 21-86
summary: In his doctoral thesis, supervised by Henri Poincaré, Bachelier asked whether the movements of French government bond prices on the Paris exchange could be described with probability theory. He assumed that at any moment the speculator's expected gain is zero, so a price is as likely to move for as against a trader, and that a price change over a period is the sum of many small independent shocks. From this he derived, five years before Einstein's 1905 work on Brownian motion, what is now called a random walk in continuous time: the probability of each future price follows a bell curve centred on today's price, and its spread widens with the square root of the time elapsed. Rule: standard deviation of the price change over t days = sigma * sqrt(t), so quadrupling the horizon only doubles the typical move. He used these results to value options and other conditional contracts and compared his figures with prices quoted in the market. Economists largely ignored the thesis until Leonard Savage and Paul Samuelson drew attention to it in the 1950s. Caveat: his model lets prices become negative and makes the size of moves independent of the price level; Samuelson and others replaced it with geometric (log-price) Brownian motion, and Mandelbrot later showed that real price changes contain far more extreme moves than the bell curve allows.

title: The Behavior of Stock-Market Prices
summary: Fama's doctoral study asked two questions about the daily prices of the thirty stocks in the Dow Jones Industrial Average: are successive price changes independent of one another, as the random-walk model says, and what shape does the distribution of those changes have? Using serial correlation coefficients, runs tests and filter rules (trading rules that buy after a rise of a set percentage and sell after a fall), he found that past changes carried almost no usable information about future changes, and that the filter rules did not beat simply buying and holding once trading costs were counted. On shape, the distributions were more peaked in the middle and had far more very large moves than a normal (bell-curve) distribution, which he read as support for Mandelbrot's stable Paretian hypothesis. Random-walk rule: price tomorrow = price today + an independent random step, so charts of past prices cannot forecast the next step. The paper set the empirical agenda that grew into the efficient-market hypothesis. Caveat: later studies with larger samples and sharper tests found small but statistically reliable patterns, such as short-term reversals in individual stocks and momentum over several months, and the infinite-variance stable model was largely abandoned because the variance of returns appears finite and long-horizon returns look closer to normal.

title: Efficient Capital Markets: A Review of Theory and Empirical Work
summary: This review defined an efficient market as one in which prices always fully reflect the information available, and organised two decades of evidence around three versions of the claim. The weak form says past prices and returns cannot be used to earn excess returns; the semi-strong form adds all public information, such as earnings or stock-split announcements; the strong form adds information held privately by insiders or professionals. Fama concluded that the weak and semi-strong forms were well supported: serial correlations were tiny, trading rules failed after costs, and event studies showed prices adjusting quickly to news. The strong form held for professional money managers, whose funds did not beat the market on average, but failed for corporate insiders and for stock-exchange specialists with privileged access to order information. Rule: E[return(t+1) | information at t] = equilibrium expected return, so returns in excess of that are a fair game with zero mean. Fama noted that testing this needs a model of what returns should be, so every test is also a test of that model, a point later called the joint-hypothesis problem. Caveat: Grossman and Stiglitz argued that perfectly efficient markets are impossible because nobody would then pay to gather information, and later decades produced many apparent anomalies (size, value, momentum) whose interpretation still turns on the joint hypothesis.

title: Stock Market Prices Do Not Follow Random Walks: Evidence from a Simple Specification Test
summary: Lo and MacKinlay asked whether weekly U.S. stock returns are consistent with a random walk, using a test built on how variance grows with the measurement horizon. If prices follow a random walk, the variance of a q-week return is exactly q times the variance of a one-week return, the variance counterpart of the square-root-of-time rule for volatility. Their statistic is the variance ratio VR(q) = Var(q-period return) / (q * Var(1-period return)), which equals 1 under a random walk; values above 1 mean returns tend to continue, values below 1 mean they tend to reverse. They derived versions of the test that remain valid when volatility changes over time, which matters for financial data. Using weekly returns from the early 1960s to the mid-1980s, they rejected the random walk for market indexes and size-sorted portfolios: weekly returns were positively autocorrelated, most strongly for portfolios of small stocks, while individual stocks showed slightly negative autocorrelation. They argued that infrequent trading of some stocks could not by itself explain the pattern. The variance ratio became a standard tool for testing predictability at different horizons. Caveat: later work attributed much of the index autocorrelation to stale prices of thinly traded stocks and other trading frictions, and the effect has been weaker in more recent data.

title: RiskMetrics—Technical Document
venue: J.P. Morgan (Morgan Guaranty Trust Company) and Reuters, New York; 4th edition, December 1996
summary: This document explained the RiskMetrics method that J.P. Morgan first published in 1994 and made freely available, together with daily data sets of volatilities and correlations, so that any institution could measure market risk the same way. The practical question was how a bank can turn thousands of positions in bonds, stocks, currencies and commodities into one number for the loss it might face over a day or a month. The answer combined a few simple choices. Returns are measured as log (continuously compounded) price changes. Volatility is estimated with an exponentially weighted moving average that gives recent days more weight: variance today = 0.94 * variance yesterday + 0.06 * yesterday's squared return for daily data, with a decay factor of 0.97 for the monthly horizon. Returns are treated as conditionally normal, so the 95 percent value at risk is 1.65 standard deviations of the portfolio's value change, with positions combined through a correlation matrix. Volatility for longer horizons is scaled by the square root of time, a rule the document itself says to apply with caution. Caveat: conditional normality understates how often large losses occur, square-root scaling misleads when volatility clusters, and value at risk says nothing about how large losses are once the threshold is passed, which later pushed regulators and risk managers toward expected shortfall.

title: Scale Models
venue: Risk 11, 104-107 (condensed version of Wharton Financial Institutions Center working paper 97-34, Converting 1-Day Volatility to h-Day Volatility: Scaling by Root-h is Worse than You Think)
summary: Risk managers often turn a one-day volatility into a ten-day or longer figure by multiplying it by the square root of the horizon, as bank regulators and RiskMetrics did. Diebold, Hickman, Inoue and Schuermann asked when that shortcut is valid. The rule sigma(h days) = sqrt(h) * sigma(1 day) is exact only when daily returns are independent and identically distributed. Real daily returns show volatility clustering, which they modelled with a GARCH(1,1) process, and under such a process volatility drifts back toward its long-run level as the horizon lengthens. Scaling a one-day estimate by sqrt(h) carries today's unusually high or low volatility all the way out to the long horizon, so the scaled figures swing far more than true long-horizon volatility does. Their worked comparisons showed that the resulting errors can be large, which is the point of the working paper's title. They recommended modelling volatility directly at the horizon that matters, or using formulas for aggregating GARCH processes over time (due to Drost and Nijman), rather than scaling mechanically. Caveat: the alternative depends on the GARCH model being correctly specified, and later research found that when returns contain jumps, square-root scaling can instead understate long-horizon tail risk, so the direction of the error depends on the true process.

title: The Extreme Value Method for Estimating the Variance of the Rate of Return
summary: Parkinson asked whether the daily high and low prices that markets record could estimate volatility better than closing prices alone. If a price follows a random walk without drift, the range between the highest and lowest price during a period carries more information about the variance than the net change from one close to the next, because it reflects the whole path rather than just two points on it. Using the known distribution of the range of Brownian motion, he derived the estimator: variance per period = (1 / (4 * ln 2)) * the average over periods of (ln(High / Low))^2. For the same number of days, this estimate has a much smaller sampling error than the usual close-to-close estimator, so far fewer observations are needed for a given precision, which is valuable because volatility changes over time and old data become less relevant. Volatility is the square root of this variance and can be annualized like any other estimate. The idea showed that cheap, widely published data contained more information about risk than standard practice was using. Caveat: the method assumes continuous trading, no overnight gaps and no drift; because recorded highs and lows come from discrete trades and miss moves while the market is closed, it tends to understate true volatility, which motivated later refinements by Garman and Klass, Rogers and Satchell, and Yang and Zhang.

title: On the Estimation of Security Price Volatilities from Historical Data
summary: Garman and Klass asked how to get the most accurate volatility estimate from the four prices commonly reported for each trading day: open, high, low and close. Building on Parkinson's range estimator and assuming the log price follows a driftless random walk, they derived combinations of these prices that minimise the sampling variance of the estimate, and showed that the best ones are several times more efficient than using closing prices alone, so a few weeks of data can do the work of months. The version most used in practice is: daily variance = 0.5 * (ln(High / Low))^2 - (2 * ln 2 - 1) * (ln(Close / Open))^2, averaged over days. The first term uses the intraday range, and the second removes the part of the range that the open-to-close move already explains. They also discussed how to handle the hours when the market is closed, since an overnight jump between one close and the next open is invisible to the intraday prices and must be measured separately. Caveat: like Parkinson's estimator, it assumes continuous trading and no drift, so it is biased when prices trend strongly or trade infrequently; Rogers and Satchell (1991) and Yang and Zhang (2000) proposed estimators that allow for drift and opening jumps, and the choice of estimator matters most for illiquid assets.

title: Mutual Fund Performance
summary: Sharpe asked how to judge whether a mutual fund manager did a good job, given that a fund can earn more simply by taking more risk. Drawing on the new capital asset pricing theory, he proposed the reward-to-variability ratio, now called the Sharpe ratio: SR = (average fund return - risk-free interest rate) / standard deviation of the fund's return. The numerator is the reward for bearing risk and the denominator is the total risk taken, so the ratio measures excess return per unit of volatility. A fund with a higher ratio lets an investor, by mixing it with borrowing or lending, get a better return for any chosen level of risk. He applied the measure to annual returns of 34 open-end mutual funds over 1954 to 1963 and compared it with Treynor's measure, which uses sensitivity to the market instead of total volatility. Most funds did worse than the Dow Jones Industrial Average on this basis, rankings showed only partial persistence, and funds with higher expense ratios tended to perform worse, suggesting that the average manager did not add enough to cover costs. Caveat: standard deviation treats gains and losses alike and assumes returns are roughly normal; strategies that sell options, or returns that are smoothed, can show a flattering ratio that hides crash risk, and estimated ratios carry large sampling error.

title: The Sharpe Ratio
summary: Almost thirty years after introducing the measure, Sharpe wrote this article to state precisely what it is, when it should be used and how it is often misused. He defined it on the differential return, d = fund return - benchmark return (the benchmark is usually a riskless asset but can be another portfolio), so the ratio = average of d / standard deviation of d. He distinguished the ex ante version, built from forecasts and used to choose investments, from the ex post version computed from history. He showed that if differential returns are independent over time, the ratio grows with the square root of the measurement interval, so a monthly ratio is multiplied by sqrt(12) to annualize, and ratios must be compared over the same interval. He stressed that ranking by the ratio is right when the investor will hold just one of the candidates, combined with borrowing or lending, but not when the candidate will be added to an existing portfolio, because its correlation with that portfolio then matters. When the benchmark is another risky portfolio, the same calculation gives what is often called an information ratio. Caveat: the sqrt(12) annualization fails when returns are autocorrelated, as Lo (2002) showed, and the ratio says nothing about skewness, fat tails or how many strategies were tried before the reported one was chosen.

title: The Statistics of Sharpe Ratios
summary: Lo asked how accurate a Sharpe ratio estimated from historical returns really is. Because the mean and the standard deviation are both estimated from a finite sample, the ratio itself is a noisy statistic, and Lo derived its sampling distribution. For returns that are independent and identically distributed, the standard error of the estimated ratio is SE ~ sqrt((1 + 0.5 * SR^2) / T), where SR is the ratio per period and T is the number of observations; this lets an analyst put a confidence interval around a reported figure. He then showed what happens when returns are serially correlated, as is common for hedge funds whose holdings are illiquid or whose reported returns are smoothed: the usual practice of multiplying a monthly ratio by sqrt(12) to annualize can be badly wrong, and with positive autocorrelation it overstates the annual ratio. He gave a corrected scaling factor that depends on the autocorrelations and applied it to mutual fund and hedge fund data, showing that rankings of funds can change after the correction. Caveat: the formulas rely on large-sample approximations; later work by Mertens and by Opdyke showed that skewness and fat tails also widen the error, and none of these corrections accounts for selection among many tested strategies, which the deflated Sharpe ratio later addressed.

title: Diversification Returns and Asset Contributions
summary: Booth and Fama asked how each asset in a portfolio contributes to the portfolio's compound (geometric) growth rate, which is what an investor's wealth actually experiences over time. They used the approximation that a compound return is about equal to the average (arithmetic) return minus half the variance: compound return ~ mean - variance / 2. Because diversification pushes portfolio variance below the weighted average of the assets' variances while leaving the average return unchanged, a regularly rebalanced portfolio compounds faster than the weighted average of its assets' compound returns. They called the gap the diversification return: 0.5 * (weighted average of asset variances - portfolio variance). They then showed how to split this among the assets, so that an asset's contribution to portfolio growth equals its own compound return plus a term that is larger when the asset is volatile but only weakly correlated with the rest of the portfolio. This explains why adding a volatile asset with a modest compound return can still raise a portfolio's compound growth, and why volatility is a drag on compounding in the first place. Caveat: the extra growth relies on rebalancing back to fixed weights and on the variance approximation, which loosens for large returns; later work stressed that it does not raise expected arithmetic returns, and it shrinks after trading costs and taxes.

title: Portfolio Selection
summary: Markowitz asked how an investor should choose a portfolio, and rejected the then-common advice to put money where the expected return is highest, because that rule would never recommend diversification. He proposed that investors care about two things: the expected return of the whole portfolio and its variance, which measures how widely results can scatter. The portfolio's expected return is the weighted average of the assets' expected returns, but its variance depends on how the assets move together: portfolio variance = the sum over every pair of assets i and j of w_i * w_j * covariance(i, j). Because covariances, not just individual variances, drive total risk, combining assets that are not perfectly correlated reduces risk without necessarily giving up return, which is the mathematical case for diversification. The investor should consider only efficient portfolios, those with the least variance for a given expected return (or the most return for a given variance), and pick among them according to his or her taste for risk. He illustrated the efficient set geometrically for three and four securities. Caveat: in practice the inputs must be estimated, and the optimizer leans heavily on assets whose expected returns happen to be overestimated; later studies found that estimated mean-variance portfolios often do no better out of sample than simple equal weighting, and variance counts upside surprises as risk.

title: An Analytic Derivation of the Efficient Portfolio Frontier
venue: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis 7(4), 1851-1872
summary: Merton asked for an exact mathematical description of the efficient frontier when investors may buy, or sell short, any amount of each risky asset, replacing the graphs and numerical searches used before. Using calculus with constraints, he showed that the minimum possible variance for a target expected return mu is a quadratic function of mu. Writing V for the covariance matrix, m for the vector of expected returns and 1 for a vector of ones, define a = 1'V^-1 1, b = 1'V^-1 m, c = m'V^-1 m and d = a * c - b^2; then the smallest variance = (a * mu^2 - 2 * b * mu + c) / d. On a chart of standard deviation against expected return this frontier is a hyperbola, and its leftmost point, the global minimum-variance portfolio, has variance 1 / a and expected return b / a. He proved that every frontier portfolio is a mix of any two distinct frontier portfolios (two-fund separation), and that adding a riskless asset turns the frontier into a straight line starting at the risk-free rate, the line on which capital market theory is built. The closed form makes it easy to see how the frontier responds to changes in the inputs. Caveat: the formula requires unrestricted short selling and known means and covariances; with no-short-sale limits a numerical solver is needed, and errors in estimating m dominate real applications.

title: How Many Stocks Make a Diversified Portfolio?
venue: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis 22(3), 353-363
summary: Statman asked how many randomly chosen stocks an investor needs before further diversification stops being worthwhile. Earlier work, notably Evans and Archer (1968), suggested that about ten stocks captured most of the benefit. Statman compared the marginal benefit of adding a stock, lower portfolio risk, valued by how much extra expected return the investor could earn by borrowing or lending to get back to the original risk level, with its marginal cost, the extra transaction costs compared with a low-cost index fund. For an equally weighted portfolio of n stocks, variance = average covariance + (average variance - average covariance) / n, so the stock-specific part of risk fades like 1/n while market-wide risk remains. Under his assumptions, diversification kept paying for itself well beyond ten stocks: he concluded that a well-diversified portfolio of randomly chosen stocks needs at least 30 stocks for an investor who borrows and at least 40 for one who lends. Caveat: the answer depends on how volatile individual stocks are relative to the market, and Campbell, Lettau, Malkiel and Xu (2001) found that idiosyncratic volatility had risen over time, implying that around 50 stocks were needed for similar diversification in their later sample; studies focused on long-horizon shortfall risk suggest even more.

title: Toward Maximum Diversification
summary: Choueifaty and Coignard asked how to build an equity portfolio that is as diversified as possible without forecasting returns. They defined the diversification ratio of a long-only portfolio: DR = (sum of each weight * that asset's volatility) / (volatility of the portfolio). The numerator is what the portfolio's risk would be if all assets were perfectly correlated, so DR equals 1 for a single stock and rises as holdings offset one another. The most diversified portfolio is the one that maximises DR. They showed it has a distinctive property: every asset held has the same correlation with the portfolio, and any asset left out is more highly correlated with the portfolio than those included. Maximising DR is equivalent to maximising the Sharpe ratio if every asset's expected return is proportional to its volatility, so the method amounts to assuming that all stocks offer the same return per unit of risk. In their backtests on U.S. and euro-area stock universes, the portfolio delivered higher Sharpe ratios than market-capitalisation-weighted indexes and compared well with minimum-variance portfolios. Caveat: the authors' firm, TOBAM, manages funds built on this method; the backtest advantage depends on the period, universe and constraints chosen, and the portfolio can concentrate in a small number of weakly correlated holdings.

title: A Simplified Model for Portfolio Analysis
summary: Markowitz's method needed a covariance for every pair of securities, which for a hundred stocks means nearly five thousand numbers and, in 1963, expensive computer time. Sharpe asked whether a simpler description of how securities move together could give nearly the same portfolios at a fraction of the cost. He assumed each security's return is linked to a single common index, such as the level of the stock market, plus an independent part of its own: return_i = a_i + b_i * index return + e_i, where the e terms of different securities are uncorrelated. Then the covariance of two securities is just b_i * b_j * variance(index), so the analyst needs only an intercept, a slope and a residual variance for each security plus the index's mean and variance, roughly 3n + 2 inputs instead of n(n - 1)/2 covariances. He showed that the computation became dramatically faster and that the resulting portfolios were close to those of the full model in a test example. The slope b_i, estimated by regressing a security's returns on the index, is what became known as beta. Caveat: the assumption that the residuals are uncorrelated is false in practice, because industry and style effects make stocks co-move beyond the market, which led to multi-factor models such as Rosenberg's, and estimated betas drift over time.

title: Capital Asset Prices: A Theory of Market Equilibrium under Conditions of Risk
summary: Sharpe asked what asset prices must look like if every investor chooses portfolios the way Markowitz recommended. He assumed investors care only about expected return and risk, agree on the probabilities, and can borrow or lend freely at one riskless interest rate. Then everyone holds the same combination of risky assets, mixed with borrowing or lending to suit their taste for risk, so in equilibrium that combination must be the whole market, and efficient portfolios lie on a straight line from the riskless rate (the capital market line). For individual assets only the part of risk that moves with the market is rewarded, because the rest can be diversified away. In the notation that later became standard: expected return of asset i = risk-free rate + beta_i * (expected market return - risk-free rate), where beta_i = covariance(asset i, market) / variance(market). The model, reached independently by Lintner, Mossin and Treynor, gave finance its first equilibrium theory of risk and return and the language of systematic versus diversifiable risk. Caveat: tests from the 1970s onward found the relation between beta and average return much flatter than predicted, Fama and French (1992) found little relation at all once size and value were accounted for, and Roll (1977) argued that the model cannot be tested properly because the true market portfolio is unobservable.

title: The Valuation of Risk Assets and the Selection of Risky Investments in Stock Portfolios and Capital Budgets
summary: Lintner asked how a risk-averse investor should choose a stock portfolio when riskless lending and borrowing are available, and what that implies for stock prices and for companies' investment decisions. He showed that the best mix of risky stocks does not depend on the investor's wealth or attitude to risk; only the split between that mix and the riskless asset changes, a separation result that extends James Tobin's earlier work. If all investors share the same forecasts, prices must adjust until each stock's expected excess return is proportional to its covariance with the total market portfolio: expected return_i - risk-free rate = (market price of risk) * covariance(return_i, market return). This is algebraically the same as the beta form of the capital asset pricing model, so the paper, together with Sharpe (1964) and Mossin (1966), is one of the founding statements of the CAPM. He also drew out implications for how firms should evaluate risky investment projects and for the role of diversification within stock portfolios. Caveat: the model assumes unlimited borrowing at the riskless rate and identical forecasts; Fischer Black's 1972 zero-beta version drops the borrowing assumption and fits the flatter empirical risk-return line better, yet the CAPM's central prediction, that beta alone explains average returns, has fared poorly in tests.

title: The Performance of Mutual Funds in the Period 1945–1964
summary: Jensen asked whether professional mutual fund managers earned more than they should have, given the risk they took, and whether any individual fund showed true forecasting skill. Using the capital asset pricing model as the yardstick, he regressed each fund's excess return on the market's excess return: fund return - risk-free rate = alpha + beta * (market return - risk-free rate) + error. Beta captures the market risk the fund chose to take, and the intercept alpha, now called Jensen's alpha, is the average return beyond what that risk explains; a manager with genuine skill should show a positive alpha. Applied to 115 mutual funds over 1945 to 1964, the average alpha was negative after expenses, and even when expenses were added back the funds on average did not beat a buy-and-hold market portfolio of the same risk. Few funds had significantly positive alphas, and no more than chance alone would produce. He concluded that the funds showed little evidence of forecasting prices well enough to cover their costs. Caveat: alpha depends on the benchmark, and Roll later showed that an inefficient market proxy can create or hide alpha; managers who time the market have changing betas that bias the regression; and later multi-factor models attribute much apparent alpha to exposure to size, value and momentum.

title: A New Interpretation of Information Rate
summary: Kelly, an engineer at Bell Labs, asked how a gambler should bet when a private wire, possibly noisy, reports the outcomes of games before the betting closes. Maximising expected wealth would mean staking everything on each tip, which leads to ruin as soon as one tip is wrong. Kelly instead asked which betting policy makes wealth grow fastest over many repeated bets, and showed that the answer is to bet a fixed fraction of current wealth chosen to maximise the expected logarithm of wealth. For an even-money bet won with probability p and lost with probability q = 1 - p, the growth rate per bet is G(f) = p * log(1 + f) + q * log(1 - f), which is largest at f* = p - q; the general form for odds of b to 1, usually quoted as the Kelly formula, is f* = (bp - q) / b. He also showed that the maximum growth rate equals the rate at which the wire transmits information, in Claude Shannon's sense, linking gambling to information theory. The logarithm in his argument comes from compounding over repeated bets, not from a theory of utility. Caveat: full Kelly betting produces deep and long drawdowns and assumes the probabilities are known exactly; when p is overestimated it overbets, so practitioners usually stake a fraction of the Kelly amount, and Paul Samuelson argued that maximising growth is not the right goal for every investor.

title: The Kelly Criterion in Blackjack, Sports Betting, and the Stock Market
venue: Chapter 9 in Handbook of Asset and Liability Management, Vol. 1: Theory and Methodology (S. A. Zenios and W. T. Ziemba, eds.), Elsevier/North-Holland, 385-428
summary: Thorp, who used card counting to beat blackjack in the early 1960s and later ran investment partnerships, explains how the Kelly criterion works when real money is at stake. The question is how much of one's capital to risk on each favourable opportunity. The criterion says: choose the fraction f of wealth that maximises the expected logarithm of wealth, which in the long run outgrows any essentially different strategy and tends to reach a wealth target fastest. For a single bet at even odds the fraction equals the edge, p - q. For an asset with expected return mu and volatility sigma, and a riskless rate r, the continuous-time answer is f* = (mu - r) / sigma^2, and the resulting growth rate is r + (mu - r)^2 / (2 * sigma^2). A position's growth rate behaves like mean - variance / 2, which shows the drag volatility puts on compounding: betting about twice the Kelly fraction brings growth back down to the riskless rate, and betting more pushes it lower still, eventually below zero. Thorp works through blackjack, sports betting and stock-market examples and recommends betting less than full Kelly when estimates are uncertain. Caveat: the attractive properties are long-run results; over realistic horizons full Kelly carries a high chance of large drawdowns, and errors in mu or sigma are magnified because the fraction depends on their ratio.

title: Options: A Monte Carlo Approach
summary: Boyle asked how to value options when no neat formula exists, and showed that random simulation could do the job. The idea rests on risk-neutral valuation: under the conditions of the Black-Scholes argument, an option's price equals its expected payoff computed as if the underlying asset grew at the riskless rate, discounted at that rate. So one can simulate many possible paths of the asset price under that assumption, compute the option's payoff on each path, average the payoffs and discount: price ~ exp(-r * T) * (1/N) * the sum of payoffs over N simulated paths. Because the error of such an average shrinks only like 1/sqrt(N), Boyle showed how variance-reduction techniques cut the number of simulations needed, notably control variates, which use a related quantity with a known answer to correct the estimate, and antithetic sampling, which pairs each random draw with its mirror image. He illustrated the method on European call options and checked it against known analytical prices, while stressing its flexibility for more complicated payoffs and price processes. Caveat: the simple version handles options exercised only at maturity; options with early exercise, such as American puts, resisted simulation for two decades until regression-based methods, notably Longstaff and Schwartz (2001), made them practical, and convergence remains slow without variance reduction.

title: Monte Carlo Methods in Financial Engineering
venue: Springer, New York; 1st edition (series: Stochastic Modelling and Applied Probability)
summary: Glasserman's book is the standard graduate reference on using random simulation to price derivatives and measure risk. It addresses a recurring question: when a price or a risk figure is an expected value that no formula delivers, how can simulation estimate it accurately and quickly? The book covers generating random numbers and correlated normal variables; simulating Brownian motion and the stochastic differential equations of asset prices and interest rates, including discretisation schemes such as Euler and Milstein and their errors; variance-reduction methods (control variates, antithetic sampling, stratification, importance sampling); quasi-Monte Carlo methods that replace random points with evenly spread low-discrepancy sequences; estimating price sensitivities (the Greeks) by finite differences, pathwise derivatives and likelihood-ratio weights; pricing American options; and risk-management applications such as estimating value at risk and the probability of large portfolio losses. The rule that runs through it: a Monte Carlo estimate is an average of N independent samples, and its standard error = sample standard deviation / sqrt(N), so halving the error takes four times the work unless the variance is reduced. Caveat: it assumes graduate-level probability, and some major later advances, such as multilevel Monte Carlo (Giles, 2008) and adjoint algorithmic differentiation for fast Greeks, appeared after it was published.

title: The Variation of Certain Speculative Prices
summary: Mandelbrot asked whether the Gaussian (bell-curve) model of price changes, used since Bachelier, actually fits speculative prices. Studying cotton prices over long periods, along with some data on wheat, railroad stocks and interest rates, he found far too many very large changes for a normal distribution: the tails were heavy and fell off like a power law, Probability(|change| > x) roughly proportional to x^(-alpha), rather than with the bell curve's much faster decay. He proposed modelling price changes with stable Paretian (Lévy-stable) distributions, a family that includes the normal as the special case alpha = 2; for cotton he estimated alpha at about 1.7. With alpha below 2 the variance is infinite, so sample variances never settle down as more data arrive, and the shape of the distribution is the same whatever the time interval, so daily and monthly changes look alike after rescaling. He also observed that large changes tend to be followed by large changes, an early description of volatility clustering. The paper started the study of fat tails in finance. Caveat: later evidence showed that the variance of returns appears finite, with tail exponents typically around 3, and that returns over longer horizons look closer to normal, which contradicts stable laws; models with finite variance, fat tails and changing volatility now fit better.

title: Empirical Properties of Asset Returns: Stylized Facts and Statistical Issues
summary: Cont asked which statistical properties of asset returns are so common across markets, instruments and periods that any realistic model should reproduce them, and why they are hard to measure precisely. He listed a set of stylized facts. Linear autocorrelations of returns are essentially zero, except over very short intraday horizons. Return distributions have heavy tails, with a tail exponent usually between two and five, so the variance is finite but extreme moves are much more frequent than under a normal distribution. Large losses tend to be bigger than large gains. Over longer horizons returns look more nearly normal (aggregational Gaussianity). Volatility clusters: turbulent periods bunch together, and the autocorrelation of absolute or squared returns stays positive and decays slowly over weeks and months. Even after correcting for volatility clustering with GARCH-type models, the remaining shocks still have fat tails. Volatility tends to rise after prices fall (the leverage effect), and trading volume moves with volatility. Rule of thumb: corr(r_t, r_(t+k)) ~ 0, but corr(|r_t|, |r_(t+k)|) > 0 and fades slowly as k grows, so the direction of returns is hard to predict while their size is partly predictable. He also explained why estimating tail exponents and long-range dependence from finite samples is tricky. Caveat: these are descriptive regularities rather than explanations; estimates vary with method and sample, and the facts are weaker or different in some asset classes and eras.

title: Techniques for Verifying the Accuracy of Risk Measurement Models
summary: Kupiec asked how a bank or a regulator can tell, from a record of past trading results, whether a value-at-risk model is accurate. If a 99 percent one-day VaR model is right, losses should exceed the VaR on about 1 percent of days, and the number of such exceptions over T days follows a binomial distribution. His proportion-of-failures test compares the observed exception rate x / T with the promised rate p through a likelihood ratio: LR = -2 * ln[(1 - p)^(T - x) * p^x] + 2 * ln[(1 - x/T)^(T - x) * (x/T)^x], which is approximately chi-squared with one degree of freedom when the model is correct. He also proposed a test based on how long it takes until the first exception occurs. His main finding was sobering: with the samples typically available, such as one year of daily data, these tests have little power, so an accurate model and a seriously flawed one often cannot be told apart, especially at high confidence levels where exceptions are rare. Caveat: the test checks only how many exceptions occur, not whether they cluster in time or how large the losses beyond the VaR were; Christoffersen (1998) added a test for clustering, and later work also tests the size of losses in the tail.

title: Evaluating Interval Forecasts
summary: Christoffersen asked how to judge forecasts that give a range rather than a single number, such as a value-at-risk threshold that losses should breach only 1 percent of the time. He pointed out that a good interval forecast must do two things: be breached at the promised rate on average (correct unconditional coverage), and have breaches that are unpredictable rather than bunched together in turbulent periods (independence). A model that ignores volatility clustering can hit the right average rate yet fail in exactly the periods that matter most. He proposed likelihood-ratio tests for each property and a combined test of conditional coverage. The independence test treats the sequence of breaches as a two-state Markov chain and asks whether the chance of a breach today depends on whether there was one yesterday. Rule: LR(conditional coverage) = LR(unconditional coverage) + LR(independence), compared with a chi-squared distribution with two degrees of freedom. The framework became a standard part of backtesting risk models alongside Kupiec's test. Caveat: the first-order Markov test detects only day-to-day clustering and has low power against other forms of dependence; later duration-based tests examine the time between breaches, and, like Kupiec's test, it checks how often losses breach the threshold rather than how large they are.

title: Coherent Measures of Risk
summary: Artzner, Delbaen, Eber and Heath asked what properties a sensible measure of financial risk, such as a capital requirement, should have, and whether value at risk has them. They proposed four axioms. Translation invariance: adding an amount of cash to a position reduces its risk by that amount. Subadditivity: risk(X + Y) <= risk(X) + risk(Y), so merging or diversifying positions never creates extra risk. Positive homogeneity: doubling a position doubles its risk. Monotonicity: if one position always loses less than another, it is no riskier. A measure satisfying all four is called coherent. They showed that value at risk can fail subadditivity, so a VaR-based limit can sometimes be reduced just by splitting a portfolio into pieces, and that VaR ignores what happens beyond its cut-off. Coherent measures correspond to taking the worst expected loss over a set of scenarios or probability models, and tail averages such as the expected loss beyond the VaR level are coherent alternatives under standard conditions. Regulators later moved market-risk capital from VaR toward expected shortfall in the Basel trading-book reforms. Caveat: positive homogeneity ignores the extra cost of liquidating large positions, which led to convex risk measures, and expected shortfall is harder to backtest than VaR because it is not elicitable.

title: A Reality Check for Data Snooping
summary: White asked how to tell whether the best of many forecasting models or trading rules is genuinely better than a simple benchmark, or merely the luckiest of the batch. When the same data are searched repeatedly, the top performer's results are inflated by chance, a problem known as data snooping. His Reality Check tests the null hypothesis that none of the models considered beats the benchmark. For each model k it computes the average performance advantage over the benchmark, f_k; the test statistic is V = max over k of sqrt(n) * f_k, and its distribution under the null is obtained by resampling the data with a stationary bootstrap that preserves short-term dependence. Rule: judge the winning strategy against the distribution of the best result one would expect from the whole set of strategies tried, not against a single-test threshold, so the p-value accounts for every model searched. He illustrated the method with a large set of forecasting models for stock index returns, and it was soon applied to technical trading rules by Sullivan, Timmermann and White (1999). Caveat: the test needs a record of every model tried, and Hansen (2005) showed that including many poor or irrelevant models makes it overly conservative, proposing the Superior Predictive Ability test instead; stepwise methods by Romano and Wolf identify which individual models outperform.

title: A Simple, Positive Semi-Definite, Heteroskedasticity and Autocorrelation Consistent Covariance Matrix
summary: Newey and West asked how to compute reliable standard errors for regression estimates when the errors are both heteroskedastic (their variance changes over time) and autocorrelated (correlated with nearby errors), as happens with overlapping multi-period returns or persistent economic data. Ordinary least-squares standard errors assume neither problem and can then be far too small, making weak results look significant. Earlier corrections that simply summed estimated autocovariances could produce a negative variance, which is meaningless. Their estimator weights the autocovariances so that the result is always positive semi-definite. In words: the long-run variance S = Gamma_0 + the sum over lags j = 1 to L of (1 - j / (L + 1)) * (Gamma_j + Gamma_j'), where Gamma_j is the estimated covariance between terms j periods apart and the declining Bartlett weights 1 - j / (L + 1) shrink the more distant lags. The estimator is consistent when the lag window L grows slowly with the sample size. Standard errors computed this way, known as HAC (heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation consistent) or simply Newey-West standard errors, became a default in empirical finance, including in Fama-MacBeth and return-predictability regressions. Caveat: results depend on the chosen lag length, which later work by Andrews (1991) and by Newey and West (1994) made data-driven, and in small samples with highly persistent regressors the standard errors are still too small, so tests reject too often.

title: On a Measure of Lack of Fit in Time Series Models
summary: Ljung and Box asked how to check, with a single number, whether a time series, or the residuals of a fitted model, still contain autocorrelation. Box and Pierce (1970) had proposed adding up the squared sample autocorrelations over the first h lags, but in samples of realistic size that statistic tended to come out too small, so it missed real dependence. Ljung and Box corrected each term for the number of observations behind it: Q = n * (n + 2) * the sum over k = 1 to h of r_k^2 / (n - k), where n is the sample size and r_k the lag-k sample autocorrelation. If the series is white noise, Q approximately follows a chi-squared distribution with h degrees of freedom (reduced by the number of estimated ARMA parameters when testing residuals), and their simulations showed this approximation is much closer than the one for the earlier statistic. In finance the test is applied to returns to look for predictability, which would contradict a random walk, and to squared returns to look for volatility clustering. Caveat: the chi-squared reference assumes independent observations under the null; with volatility clustering, as in most return series, the test rejects too often unless a robust version is used, and the answer can depend on the number of lags h chosen.

title: A Test for Normality of Observations and Regression Residuals
summary: Jarque and Bera asked for a simple and powerful test of whether observations, or the residuals of a regression, come from a normal distribution. Working within the broad Pearson family of distributions, they derived a Lagrange multiplier test that depends only on the sample skewness S and kurtosis K: JB = (n / 6) * (S^2 + (K - 3)^2 / 4). A normal distribution has skewness 0 and kurtosis 3, so large values of JB signal departures from normality; under normality JB is approximately chi-squared with two degrees of freedom, so the 5 percent critical value is about 5.99. Their simulations showed the test had good power against a range of non-normal alternatives compared with other common tests. The test first appeared in a short 1980 note by the same authors in Economics Letters; the 1987 paper gives the full derivation and evidence. In finance it is routinely applied to returns and nearly always rejects normality for daily data because of fat tails. Caveat: the chi-squared approximation is poor in small samples, so exact or simulated critical values are needed; sample skewness and kurtosis are very sensitive to a few outliers; and a rejection says only that the data are not normal, not which distribution to use instead.

title: Distribution of the Estimators for Autoregressive Time Series with a Unit Root
venue: Journal of the American Statistical Association 74(366), 427-431
summary: Dickey and Fuller asked how to test whether a time series has a unit root, meaning it behaves like a random walk whose shocks never fade, or is stationary, meaning it tends to return to a mean. In the model y_t = rho * y_(t-1) + e_t, a unit root means rho = 1, while rho below 1 implies mean reversion. Equivalently, one regresses the change, Delta y_t = (rho - 1) * y_(t-1) + e_t, and asks whether the coefficient on the lagged level is zero. The difficulty is that under the unit-root null the usual t-statistic does not follow Student's t distribution, so standard tables reject too often. Dickey and Fuller derived the correct limiting distributions of the estimator and its t-statistic, for models without a constant, with a constant, and with a constant and a time trend, and provided critical values computed by simulation. Rule: reject a unit root only when the t-statistic is more negative than the Dickey-Fuller critical value, about -2.86 at 5 percent when a constant is included, rather than the familiar normal value of -1.65. The augmented version, which adds lagged changes to absorb short-run correlation, followed in later work. In finance the test is used on spreads and prices to check for mean reversion, for example in pairs trading. Caveat: it has low power against slow mean reversion in short samples, and structural breaks can make a stationary series look like a random walk (Perron, 1989).

title: Mean Reversion in Stock Prices: Evidence and Implications
summary: Poterba and Summers asked whether stock prices contain transitory components, temporary deviations from fundamental value that eventually reverse, and why such components would be hard to detect. They first showed that standard tests have little statistical power: a sizeable but slowly fading component could hide in return data for decades. They then applied variance-ratio tests to long histories of U.S. stock returns and to data from 17 other countries. Under a random walk the variance of k-period returns equals k times the one-period variance; they found returns positively autocorrelated over short horizons and negatively autocorrelated over horizons of several years, the signature of mean reversion. Their estimates implied that transitory components account for a large share of return variance, and they argued that changes in required returns driven by risk would struggle to explain such swings, pointing instead to slowly decaying price fads. Rule: variance ratio = Var(k-period return) / (k * Var(1-period return)); values below 1 at long horizons indicate mean reversion. Caveat: the evidence is statistically weak and leans heavily on the 1926-1946 period, which includes the Great Depression; Kim, Nelson and Startz found little mean reversion after 1946, and small-sample biases in long-horizon tests can create the appearance of reversion where none exists.

title: Evidence of Predictable Behavior of Security Returns
summary: Jegadeesh asked whether monthly returns on individual U.S. stocks can be predicted from their own past returns. Using data from the 1930s to the 1980s, he estimated how each stock's return relates to its returns in previous months and then formed portfolios based on the predicted returns. He found a strong negative relation between a stock's return in one month and its return in the next, known as short-term reversal, and a positive relation with returns about a year earlier, a pattern that foreshadowed the momentum effect. Portfolios of the stocks with the highest predicted returns beat those with the lowest by a wide and statistically significant margin, which rejected the hypothesis that individual stock prices follow random walks. Rule: in a regression of this month's return on the returns of each of the previous twelve months, the lag-1 coefficient is negative and the lag-12 coefficient positive; so last month's biggest losers tend to outperform next month, and ranking stocks by prior one-month return and taking the opposite side earns a spread. The paper helped establish that predictability in individual stocks differs by horizon: reversal over a month, continuation over a year. Caveat: later work showed that much of the one-month reversal reflects bid-ask bounce, illiquidity and short-lived price pressure, so it shrinks sharply after trading costs and is much weaker among large, liquid stocks.

title: On the Theory of the Brownian Motion
summary: Uhlenbeck and Ornstein, two physicists, asked how the velocity and position of a small particle jostled by molecules (Brownian motion) evolve over time once friction is taken into account. Einstein's earlier theory treated the particle's displacement as a pure random walk; they modelled its velocity as being continually pulled back toward zero by friction while receiving random kicks. In the notation finance later adopted, the process is dX = theta * (mu - X) * dt + sigma * dW: over a short interval, X moves back toward its long-run mean mu at a speed proportional to its distance from it, plus a random shock. Its key properties: deviations decay exponentially on average, with a half-life of ln(2) / theta; the process settles into a stationary normal distribution with variance sigma^2 / (2 * theta); and the correlation between values decays exponentially with the time between them. Over long times the particle's position still spreads out like a random walk. Finance borrowed this Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process as the standard model of mean reversion, for interest rates (Vasicek, 1977), commodity prices and the spreads between related securities in pairs trading. Caveat: applying it to markets assumes a constant mean and speed of reversion; in finite samples the estimated speed is biased upward, so mean reversion can look stronger than it is, and real spreads can stop reverting when the economic link between assets breaks.

title: Returns to Buying Winners and Selling Losers: Implications for Stock Market Efficiency
summary: Jegadeesh and Titman asked whether investors could profit by buying the stocks that had risen most over the past several months and selling those that had fallen most, in contrast with earlier studies that emphasised reversals over very short and very long horizons. Each month they ranked U.S. stocks by their returns over the previous 3 to 12 months, bought the top tenth and sold the bottom tenth, and held the positions for 3 to 12 months, overlapping portfolios formed in different months. Over 1965 to 1989 these strategies earned significant positive returns, and the profits were not explained by the stocks' market risk or by delayed reactions to common factors. Part of the gain reversed over the following two years, which they read as evidence of a delayed price response to firm-specific information rather than compensation for risk. Returns around subsequent earnings announcements showed a similar pattern. Rule: momentum return = return of the top tenth of stocks ranked by past 3-to-12-month return - return of the bottom tenth, with positions held for months rather than days. The finding became one of the most widely replicated anomalies, documented in many countries and asset classes. Caveat: high turnover means trading costs eat into momentum profits, and the strategy is prone to sudden severe crashes, especially when markets rebound sharply after a fall.

title: On Persistence in Mutual Fund Performance
summary: Carhart asked whether mutual funds that did well in one year keep doing well, as earlier studies had suggested, and whether that persistence reflects managers' skill. He built a database of funds from 1962 to 1993 that includes funds that later closed or merged, avoiding survivor bias. To measure performance he extended the Fama-French three-factor model with a fourth factor for one-year stock momentum: fund return - risk-free rate = alpha + b * market excess return + s * SMB + h * HML + p * momentum + error, where SMB is small-minus-big, HML is high-minus-low book-to-market and the momentum factor is past-year winners minus losers. He found that the apparent persistence among top funds is largely explained by their exposure to momentum stocks, often simply from holding last year's winners, and by differences in expenses and trading costs, not by stock-picking skill. The one robust persistence was at the bottom: the worst funds tended to stay poor. His four-factor model became a standard benchmark for evaluating fund managers and equity strategies. Caveat: the factors are empirical choices rather than consequences of a theory, and later evidence, such as bootstrap studies of fund alphas, suggests that a small number of managers may have genuine skill even though the average fund does not.

title: Time Series Momentum
summary: Moskowitz, Ooi and Pedersen asked whether an asset's own past return predicts its future return, as distinct from the usual cross-sectional momentum that compares assets with one another. Studying 58 liquid futures and forward contracts on equity indexes, currencies, commodities and government bonds over several decades, they found that an asset's excess return over the past 12 months positively predicted its return in the following month, with the effect lasting up to about a year and partly reversing afterwards. They called this time series momentum. A diversified strategy that goes long each contract whose past-year return was positive and short each whose return was negative, with every position scaled to the same target volatility, earned substantial returns with little exposure to standard asset-pricing factors, and did especially well during extreme market moves, including 2008. Rule: position = sign(past 12-month excess return) * (target volatility / estimated volatility of the asset). They linked the pattern to initial under-reaction followed by delayed over-reaction, and used futures-market position data to show that speculators tend to ride the trends while hedgers take the other side. Caveat: later studies argued that the evidence of predictability for individual assets is weaker than the pooled results suggest and that much of the strategy's performance comes from the volatility scaling, and trend-following funds went through a long weak stretch in the 2010s.

title: Momentum Crashes
summary: Daniel and Moskowitz asked when momentum strategies suffer their rare but devastating losses, and whether those losses can be anticipated. Studying U.S. equities back to 1927 as well as other markets and asset classes, they found that momentum crashes happen in panic states: after a prolonged market decline, while volatility is high, and at the moment the market rebounds sharply, as in 1932 and 2009. The mechanism is that after a fall the loser portfolio is full of beaten-down, high-beta stocks, so a long-winners, short-losers position is effectively short the market; when the market jumps, the losers jump most and the strategy loses heavily. In these states its payoff resembles that of a short call option on the market. Because both the bear-market condition and high volatility can be observed in advance, the authors built a dynamic strategy that scales the momentum position each month by its forecast mean divided by its forecast variance, cutting exposure in panic states and adding it in calm ones. Rule: weight on momentum = c * (forecast momentum return / forecast momentum variance), with the constant c setting overall risk. This substantially raised the Sharpe ratio relative to static momentum, with similar results across markets. Caveat: the forecasts of momentum's mean rest on a modest number of crash episodes, gains are smaller after trading costs and real-time estimation, and a simpler rule that scales by momentum's own recent volatility (Barroso and Santa-Clara, 2015) captures much of the benefit.

title: Investment Performance of Common Stocks in Relation to Their Price-Earnings Ratios: A Test of the Efficient Market Hypothesis
summary: Basu asked whether a stock's price-earnings (P/E) ratio, a piece of public information, could be used to earn returns beyond those justified by risk, which would contradict the semi-strong form of market efficiency. Using NYSE industrial firms from 1957 to 1971, he formed portfolios each year by ranking stocks on their P/E ratios and tracked their later performance. The low-P/E portfolios earned higher average returns than the high-P/E portfolios, and the difference remained after adjusting for risk with capital asset pricing model measures such as Jensen's alpha and the Sharpe and Treynor ratios. He also considered whether transaction costs, search costs and taxes would remove the advantage, concluding that a gap probably remained for some investors. Rule behind the value idea: stocks priced cheaply relative to their earnings (low P/E, or equivalently a high earnings yield, E/P = 1 / (P/E)) have tended to outperform expensive ones on average. He interpreted the result as evidence that the information in P/E ratios was not fully reflected in prices. Caveat: low-P/E stocks also tend to be smaller and more distressed, so later studies debated whether the effect is separate from the size effect; Fama and French (1992) found that book-to-market captures much of it; whether the premium compensates for risk or reflects mispricing is still contested; and value premiums were notably weak in the 2010s.

title: The Relationship between Return and Market Value of Common Stocks
summary: Banz asked whether a firm's size, measured by the market value of its common stock, helps explain average stock returns once risk is accounted for with the capital asset pricing model. Using NYSE common stocks from 1936 to 1975, he estimated a model in which expected return depends on beta and on the firm's relative market value. Smaller firms had, on average, higher risk-adjusted returns than larger firms, which became known as the size effect, and the effect had been present for at least forty years. It was not linear: it was concentrated among the very smallest firms, with little difference between average-sized and large firms. Rule: expected return = risk-free rate + beta * market premium + an extra term that is larger the smaller the firm's market value, so in that sample small capitalisation predicted higher returns. Banz was careful to say he could not tell whether size itself mattered or whether it stood in for some unknown factor correlated with size, but he concluded that the result was evidence the CAPM was misspecified. Caveat: the size premium largely faded after the early 1980s, has been concentrated in the smallest and least liquid stocks and in January, and later work argues that much of it reflects illiquidity or poor-quality firms; it shows up more reliably when firm quality is controlled for.

title: The Cross-Section of Expected Stock Returns
summary: Fama and French asked which characteristics of stocks actually explain why some earn higher average returns than others, putting the capital asset pricing model's beta in a contest with size, earnings yield, leverage and the book-to-market ratio. Using NYSE, AMEX and NASDAQ stocks from 1963 to 1990, they estimated betas carefully, forming portfolios on both size and pre-ranking beta so that beta's effect could be separated from size's, and ran Fama-MacBeth cross-sectional regressions of monthly returns on the characteristics. Once size was controlled for, beta showed essentially no relation to average return. Two easily measured variables, market equity (size) and the ratio of book equity to market equity, together captured the cross-sectional variation in average returns and absorbed the roles of leverage and earnings yield: small stocks and stocks with high book-to-market (value stocks) earned higher average returns. Rule: in monthly regressions return_i = c0 + c1 * ln(size_i) + c2 * ln(book-to-market_i) + error, the average c1 was negative and c2 positive, while beta added nothing. They suggested these variables might proxy for risk, perhaps related to financial distress. Caveat: critics argued the results could reflect data-snooping or survivorship bias in accounting data, that beta's relation to returns reappears with longer samples or annual returns, and whether the value and size premiums reward risk or reflect mispricing remains disputed.

title: Common Risk Factors in the Returns on Stocks and Bonds
summary: Fama and French asked whether a few common risk factors could explain the returns on stocks and bonds over time, following their finding that size and book-to-market predict average stock returns. They built factor-mimicking portfolios: SMB (small minus big), the return on small-company stocks minus that on large-company stocks, and HML (high minus low), the return on high book-to-market (value) stocks minus low book-to-market (growth) stocks, alongside the stock market's excess return; for bonds they added TERM (long-term minus short-term government bonds) and DEF (corporate minus government bonds). In time-series regressions on 25 portfolios sorted by size and book-to-market, the three stock factors explained most of the variation in returns, often with R-squared above 0.9, and left intercepts close to zero, meaning the model largely captured the differences in average returns. Rule (three-factor model): excess return = alpha + b * (market return - risk-free rate) + s * SMB + h * HML + error, with alpha near zero when the model prices the asset correctly. The bond factors captured common variation in bond returns, and stock returns were linked to bond returns through those shared bond-market factors. The model became the standard benchmark for measuring abnormal returns. Caveat: it fails to explain momentum and later-documented patterns related to profitability and investment, which led to four- and five-factor models, and whether SMB and HML are true risk factors or labels for mispricing remains debated.

title: Contrarian Investment, Extrapolation, and Risk
summary: Lakonishok, Shleifer and Vishny asked why value strategies, which buy stocks with low prices relative to earnings, cash flow or book value, or with low past sales growth, had outperformed glamour stocks, and whether the extra return was simply compensation for risk. Using U.S. stocks from the late 1960s to around 1990, they confirmed that value portfolios earned substantially higher returns, with the strongest results when two measures were combined, such as a low price-to-cash-flow ratio and low past sales growth. They then tested the risk explanation directly: value stocks did not underperform in the states of the world where risk should hurt, such as falling markets and recessions, and if anything did relatively well. Their explanation was behavioural: investors extrapolate past growth too far into the future, overpaying for firms that have grown fast and underpricing firms that have done poorly, while the later growth of the two groups turned out much closer than prices had implied. Rule: rank stocks on ratios such as cash flow / price or book value / market value and on past sales growth, then buy the cheap, slow-growth group and avoid the expensive, fast-growth group whose prices embed over-optimistic extrapolation. Caveat: Fama and French countered that value stocks carry distress risk that these tests miss, the risk-versus-mispricing debate is unresolved, and value strategies suffered a long and deep drawdown in the 2010s, so the premium is far from guaranteed.

title: Risk and the Rate of Return on Financial Assets: Some Old Wine in New Bottles
venue: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis 10(5), 775-784
summary: Haugen and Heins asked whether riskier stocks and portfolios have actually earned higher returns, as the theory of a positive risk-return trade-off predicts. Using several decades of U.S. stock data up to the early 1970s, they formed portfolios with different levels of risk, measured by the variance of monthly returns and by beta, and compared their realised average returns. They found no support for the idea that the market rewarded bearing this risk: over the long run, portfolios with lower variance earned average returns at least as high as, and often higher than, their riskier counterparts. Since a positive risk premium is central to both portfolio theory and the capital asset pricing model, they argued that this conventional assumption deserved rethinking. Rule of the low-volatility anomaly: theory says average return should rise with risk, but across stock portfolios the slope of average return on volatility or beta has been about zero or negative. The paper drew limited attention for many years but anticipated the later literature on low-risk investing, and Haugen went on to advocate low-volatility strategies. Caveat: the portfolio construction and statistics were simple by later standards; subsequent studies confirmed the pattern with better methods but found it concentrated among the most volatile, often small and illiquid, stocks, and partly linked to exposures such as value, profitability and interest-rate sensitivity.

title: The Cross-Section of Volatility and Expected Returns
summary: Ang, Hodrick, Xing and Zhang asked whether volatility, both market-wide and stock-specific, is priced in the cross-section of U.S. stock returns. First, they measured each stock's sensitivity to daily changes in market volatility, using changes in the VXO implied-volatility index as a proxy. Stocks whose returns rise when market volatility jumps act as insurance against bad times, and these stocks earned lower average returns, consistent with investors paying for protection against volatility risk. Second, and more surprisingly, stocks with high idiosyncratic volatility, measured as the standard deviation of the daily residuals e in r - r_f = a + b * MKT + s * SMB + h * HML + e over the past month, had very low subsequent average returns, so the most volatile group did markedly worse than the least volatile. This idiosyncratic volatility puzzle was not explained by size, book-to-market, momentum, liquidity, trading volume, coskewness or dispersion in analysts' forecasts. Rule: in their sample, high recent stock-specific volatility predicted low, not high, future returns. The paper became a cornerstone of the low-risk anomaly literature. Caveat: later work found the result sensitive to methodological choices such as portfolio weighting and how volatility is measured, explained part of it by short-term return reversal and by investors' taste for lottery-like stocks with extreme daily gains, and found that expected, rather than lagged, idiosyncratic volatility can relate positively to returns.

title: Benchmarks as Limits to Arbitrage: Understanding the Low-Volatility Anomaly
summary: Baker, Bradley and Wurgler asked why the low-volatility anomaly, the long-standing tendency of low-risk stocks to earn returns as high as or higher than high-risk stocks, has persisted even though it is well known. Using U.S. stock data from the late 1960s to 2008, they confirmed that portfolios of low-volatility and low-beta stocks delivered both lower risk and higher returns than portfolios of high-volatility and high-beta stocks. They offered a two-part explanation. On the demand side, many investors are drawn to volatile stocks because of a preference for lottery-like payoffs, a tendency to treat exciting success stories as typical (representativeness) and overconfidence, which bids up their prices. On the supply side, the professionals who could correct the mispricing are judged against capitalisation-weighted benchmarks; for a manager judged by information ratio = (return - index return) / tracking error, buying low-beta stocks adds tracking error and tends to lag in rising markets, so the benchmark itself discourages exploiting the anomaly, a limit to arbitrage. Rule: a fixed benchmark mandate makes low-risk stocks look unattractive to managers even when they offer a better return per unit of absolute risk. Caveat: the evidence is historical and partly overlaps with value, profitability and interest-rate exposures, and the popularity of low-volatility funds after this paper may have reduced the premium by raising the valuations of low-risk stocks.

title: Betting Against Beta
summary: Frazzini and Pedersen asked why high-beta assets have earned less than the capital asset pricing model predicts, and proposed an answer based on borrowing limits. Many investors, such as individuals, pension funds and mutual funds, cannot or will not borrow. To reach a higher return target they overweight risky, high-beta assets instead of leveraging safe ones, which pushes up the prices of high-beta assets and lowers their future returns, flattening the relation between beta and return. Their model predicts the effect is stronger when funding is tight. To test it they built a betting-against-beta (BAB) factor: a portfolio that holds low-beta assets leveraged up to a beta of 1 and shorts high-beta assets scaled down to a beta of 1, so its overall market exposure is about zero. Rule: BAB return = (1 / beta_low) * (low-beta excess return) - (1 / beta_high) * (high-beta excess return). The factor earned significant risk-adjusted returns in U.S. equities, in many international stock markets, and in Treasury bonds, corporate bonds and futures, and its returns were lower when funding conditions worsened, as the theory predicts. Caveat: Novy-Marx and Velikov (2022) argued that much of BAB's performance comes from unusual construction choices, including rank weighting and beta shrinkage that overweight tiny stocks, and that implementable versions earn much less; others attribute the pattern to time-varying betas.

title: Extra-Market Components of Covariance in Security Returns
venue: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis 9(2), 263-274
summary: Rosenberg asked how to describe the way security returns move together more accurately than the single-index (market) model, which assumes that, once the market's influence is removed, stocks are unrelated. He showed that returns share substantial extra-market components of covariance: stocks in the same industry, or with similar characteristics, move together beyond what the market factor explains, so the single-index model misstates portfolio risk. He proposed representing these shared movements with a modest number of common factors tied to industries and company characteristics, which lets the full covariance matrix be estimated with far fewer free parameters than estimating every pair separately. Rule: return_i = the sum over factors k of (exposure of stock i to factor k) * (return of factor k) + specific return_i, so the covariance matrix = exposures * factor covariance * exposures transposed + a diagonal matrix of stock-specific variances. In related work he predicted exposures such as beta from fundamental company descriptors rather than from each stock's own price history. Rosenberg founded Barra, whose commercial multi-factor risk models built on this approach and became an industry standard for measuring portfolio risk. Caveat: the choice of factors and descriptors involves judgment, factor structures shift over time, and such models tend to underestimate risk in crises, when correlations rise suddenly and stock-specific risks start moving together.

title: Risk, Return, and Equilibrium: Empirical Tests
summary: Fama and MacBeth asked whether the capital asset pricing model's main predictions hold in NYSE data: that expected return rises linearly with beta, that nothing besides beta (such as beta squared or a stock's own residual risk) matters systematically, and that the reward for bearing beta risk is positive. Their method became a standard tool. Each month they ran a cross-sectional regression of returns on estimated betas and the other variables, producing a series of monthly slope estimates; they then averaged each slope over time and judged its significance with a t-statistic computed from the month-to-month variation of the estimates. Rule: t-statistic = average of the monthly slopes / (standard deviation of the monthly slopes / sqrt(number of months)). To reduce errors in the estimated betas they grouped stocks into portfolios ranked on betas estimated in an earlier period. Over 1935 to 1968 they found a positive average relation between beta and return, no systematic effect of beta squared or residual risk, and an intercept above the riskless rate, which fits Black's zero-beta version of the model better than the original. Caveat: the standard errors ignore the fact that betas are themselves estimated (Shanken's 1992 correction addresses this) and are biased when regression residuals are correlated over time, and data after 1963 showed a much flatter relation between beta and return.

title: The Arbitrage Theory of Capital Asset Pricing
summary: Ross asked whether a theory of asset prices could be built without the strong assumptions of the capital asset pricing model, such as mean-variance preferences and an observable market portfolio. He assumed only that returns are generated by a linear factor model, return_i = expected return_i + the sum over k of b_ik * f_k + e_i, where the f_k are a few common factors with zero mean, the b_ik are each asset's sensitivities to them, and the e_i are asset-specific shocks that wash out in large, diversified portfolios. If investors could form a portfolio with no net cost and no factor exposure that still earned a positive expected return, that would be close to an arbitrage. Ruling out such opportunities forces expected returns to line up with factor sensitivities: expected return_i ~ lambda_0 + the sum over k of b_ik * lambda_k, where lambda_0 is the riskless (or zero-beta) rate and lambda_k is the risk premium per unit of exposure to factor k. The arbitrage pricing theory thus explains why only common, undiversifiable risks should carry a premium, without singling out the market portfolio.
